verdict: Caution: lend selectively to Leh pashmina/carpet units with verified buyer orders and clean receivables; avoid small loss-making weavers until order books and cash cycles are proven.
title: Leh Handicrafts & Carpets: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**Leh handicrafts and carpets is a wool-to-cash business: raw pashmina and wool bought from nomadic herders, spun and woven by household artisans, then sold to buyers in metros or abroad.** Cash sits in slow-moving finished stock and in receivables from distant buyers, not in the loom. The value is in design, finishing and buyer access; the weaving itself is low-margin piece work. So when a proposal lands, check where the borrower actually sits in that chain — raw wool trader, weaver, or finished-goods seller — because the working-capital cycle and the pricing power are completely different at each step.

## Where value and cash sit
**Capex is light (looms, a small workshop, maybe a dyeing unit), so the real funding need is working capital, and the real risk is inventory.** Rating work on comparable textile and craft businesses flags inventory management as a key sensitivity [9] and notes the weaving business is fixed- as well as working-capital intensive [8]. Pricing power is thin for plain weaving and stronger for branded, design-led pashmina. So ask for the buyer list and order confirmations; if the borrower cannot name repeat buyers, treat the stock as illiquid and size the limit to what the buyer orders support.

## What has changed now
**The local signal is positive but thin: Ladakhi brands showcased local craftsmanship at Lakmé Fashion Week with UT Administration support [1][2], and there is a policy push to lift pashmina from nomadic pastures into global supply chains [3].** That is visibility, not yet orders — no local sales or export figure for Leh appears in these sources, so collect from customer. Peer results are weak: Golden Carpets posted a Q1FY27 net loss of ₹7.31 lakh with revenue down 53.6% YoY to ₹12.05 lakh [5], and Priti International's revenue contracted 66.59% YoY with operating margin at -3.78% in Q1 FY27 [4]. Nationally, exports rose 32.5% Apr-to-date in USD [D], but bank credit grew 26.8% YoY against output of 3.8% [D] — money is chasing this sector faster than it is producing.

## Who to pursue, who to avoid
**Pursue established Leh sellers with named buyers, repeat orders and a design or brand story — the type now getting fashion-week exposure [1][2].** Avoid pure job-work weavers and traders with no buyer contracts; the peer losses above [4][5] show how fast fixed costs bite when orders stop. Note the sources say little specifically about Leh volumes, so lean on first principles and these peers.
Rating methodology ties comfort to low leverage and longer-tenure debt [10], and to liquidity to meet short-term needs [11] — so keep the limit short-tenure and self-liquidating.
watch: Top buyer share above half of sales -> seek a second confirmed buyer before renewal
Cheque returns or delayed buyer payments -> cut limit and ask for order confirmations
Finished stock value exceeds order book -> revalue stock and reduce limit
